steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our HCI paper on designing an LLM-powered question-answering chatbot for online news. It should motivate why readers and newsrooms want to engage through questions, discuss chatbots and LLMs in the news industry, and summarize our interview study with journalists, our online experiment with readers, the main findings, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Readers have questions after reading news; journalists can't answer them all; both sides want dialogue
- LLMs and chatbots in the news industry; QA remains a challenge; need to understand journalists' and readers' needs
- Our goal (QA chatbots) and the interview study with journalists
- The MTurk experiment with readers and its findings
- Implications and contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Journalists and reporters integrate information and interpretation carefully in a news article to inform readers about a topic, event, or phenomenon in a balanced and objective way. Still, prior research shows that readers often are left with questions for the journalists/authors after reading news. Readers use different means like news comment sections, email, and social media direct messages to ask their questions. But for many reasons like the abundance of questions, lack of time, and absence of direct incentives, journalists cannot respond to the queries. On the other hand, journalists and newsrooms both are interested in engaging with the audience/readers, to learn which aspects of their news raised curiosity and questions in readers' minds, and to understand if readers are questioning the newsroom's journalistic integrity. This knowledge is important for learning what attracts readers to news content, targeting the right audience for news recommendations, building trust with the audience and so on. Meier et al. say that “a paradigm shift away from a ‘ lecturing ’ approach to a ‘ dialogue ’ approach is a key factor for journalism in a post-truth era”. So there is clearly an interest from both readers and newsrooms to engage with each other in a dialogue through question-answering.

With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), the news media industry, like any other industry, is also looking at how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and LLMs can be integrated with news production, distribution, audience engagement, and other related processes to improve efficiency, increase trust and accountability, and open new possibilities. For example, BBC has started experimenting with how bot technologies can be used to reach new audiences on messaging platforms and social media. They developed a prototype of an in-article chatbot to help less engaged audiences understand big news stories. Other media outlets started experimenting with Meta (previously known as Facebook) chatbots. These experiments are going on individually in different newsrooms, but facilitating question-answering (QA), which is one of the primary modes of interaction and dialogue in chatbots, is still a challenge for newsrooms. Researchers are working on reducing technological limitations like the lack of truthfulness and the existence of biased and formulaic text in LLM responses, but we argue that it is also important to take a systematic approach to understand how journalists and readers want to use a chatbot for question-answering and what roles they think fit such a chatbot. For example, are journalists comfortable with a chatbot answering readers' questions about the news article they wrote? What types of questions do readers expect the chatbot to answer? And what types of questions do they expect the authors to answer? If we don't answer these questions, we may end up designing QA chatbots that are detached from the needs of readers and newsrooms.

This paper takes a formative step towards designing LLM-powered chatbots that can answer open-ended questions from readers, reduce the burden on journalists of answering a large number of queries, and at the same time elevate communication between readers and journalists. We call these chatbots QA chatbots. In the rest of the paper we use the terms QA chatbots and chatbots interchangeably for chatbots that can answer questions from news readers, unless we say otherwise. We only focus on question-answering in the context of LLMs, but in a real-world setting, like many LLM-powered chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT), a QA chatbot (or just a chatbot) will likely have other forms of interaction too (e.g., recommending news). For our research agenda we conducted two studies. First, we interviewed six professional journalists to understand how journalists answer questions from readers now and, more broadly, how they interact with readers. The interviews showed that most journalists now get feedback and answer readers' questions through one-to-one conversations over email, direct messages, or in-person meetups, apart from a few member gatherings that news outlets organize. All participants were enthusiastic about using a QA chatbot as a mediator between them and readers. They want the chatbot to answer the factual and redundant questions from readers, while questions seeking subjective interpretation should be directed to them.

- Experiment with readers
  - between-subject experiment on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), 124 participants
  - goals: (1) match between readers' perspectives and journalists' view; (2) how chatbot modulates questioning patterns (prior work: chatbots modulate user behaviour)
  - three articles (health, politics, environment); questions to authors or chatbot
  - grounded theory + quantitative measures
  - Information (short-form factual, long-form details) vs Interpretation (explanation, opinion)
  - facts more to chatbot; explanation/opinion with multiple facets more to authors
- Implications
  - partial match with journalists; but many readers asked subjective questions to chatbot, wanted authors to answer factual too
  - chatbot modulates behavior: low perceived quality -> critical of integrity only when authors in loop
- Contributions
  - need to understand perspectives; devise/communicate policies; framework for QA chatbot policy
  - (1) interviews with six journalists; (2) experiment with 124 participants; (3) design framework

And what types of questions do they expect the authors to answer? If we don't answer these questions, we may end up designing QA chatbots that are detached from the needs of readers and newsrooms.

This paper takes a formative step towards designing LLM-powered chatbots that can answer open-ended questions from readers, reduce the burden on journalists of answering a large number of queries, and at the same time elevate communication between readers and journalists. We call these chatbots QA chatbots. In the rest of the paper we use the terms QA chatbots and chatbots interchangeably for chatbots that can answer questions from news readers, unless we say otherwise. We only focus on question-answering in the context of LLMs, but in a real-world setting, like many LLM-powered chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT), a QA chatbot (or just a chatbot) will likely have other forms of interaction too (e.g., recommending news). For our research agenda we conducted two studies. First, we interviewed six professional journalists to understand how journalists answer questions from readers now and, more broadly, how they interact with readers. The interviews showed that most journalists now get feedback and answer readers' questions through one-to-one conversations over email, direct messages, or in-person meetups, apart from a few member gatherings that news outlets organize. All participants were enthusiastic about using a QA chatbot as a mediator between them and readers. They want the chatbot to answer the factual and redundant questions from readers, while questions seeking subjective interpretation should be directed to them.

Then we conducted a between-subject experiment on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) with 124 participants. It had two goals: (1) to understand to what extent readers' perspectives and questioning patterns match how journalists see the functionalities of a QA chatbot; and (2) to understand how a QA chatbot might modulate readers' questioning patterns. The second goal comes from prior research showing that chatbots can significantly modulate user behaviour. In the study participants read three articles from three different domains (health, politics, and environment) and asked questions to the authors of the articles or to a chatbot. We analyzed the responses with a grounded theory approach and a set of quantitative measures. Our findings suggest that readers mostly asked questions in two broad categories: Information, which are questions seeking short-form factual and long-form details; and Interpretation, which are questions seeking explanation and opinion. We found that the questioning patterns of readers differ significantly depending on the receiver, authors vs. chatbot. Participants asked fact-seeking questions to the chatbot more often than to the authors. On the other hand, they asked questions seeking explanation and opinion with multiple facets more often to the authors than to the chatbot.

These results show that readers' perspectives about the role of QA chatbots match the views of journalists to some extent. Readers also mostly want the chatbot to answer factual questions and want to have subjective conversations with journalists. But even with this alignment, we found evidence that a significant number of readers do not think chatbots should only answer factual questions. For example, readers did ask a considerable amount of questions seeking subjective interpretation to the chatbot, though not as often as to the authors. In the same way, a considerable number of readers wanted authors to answer factual questions as well as subjective ones. Finally, we found that chatbots can significantly modulate readers' behavior, and researchers and news organizations should be aware of this. For example, when articles had lower perceived quality, readers were motivated to be critical and question journalistic integrity when the authors were in the loop. But when the chatbot was there, readers did not engage at the same level, even when the perceived quality of the article was low.

Overall, the results show that researchers and news organizations need to understand the perspectives and expectations of journalists and readers thoroughly before deciding what a QA chatbot should do. They also show that policies around chatbots need to be devised and communicated effectively to journalists and readers. We end the paper by proposing a framework for devising a policy for designing QA chatbots for online news. Our contributions are: (1) An interview study with six journalists about their current practices and challenges in answering readers' questions and how they see the role of an intelligent chatbot for this; (2) An online experiment with 124 participants about what questions readers typically ask about a news article and how the questions change when a chatbot is at the receiving end instead of the authors; and (3) A design framework for developing a chatbot policy, based on the interviews, the online experiment, and a literature review.

steps.text:
Journalists and reporters carefully integrate information and interpretation in a news article to inform readers about a topic, event, or phenomenon in a balanced and objective manner [1,2,3,4]. Nonetheless, prior research shows that readers are often left with questions for journalists/authors after reading news [5,6]. Readers use various means such as news comment sections, email, and social media direct messages to ask their questions [7,8]. However, for many reasons, such as the abundance of questions, lack of time, and absence of direct incentives, journalists cannot respond to the queries [9,10]. On the other hand, both journalists and newsrooms have an interest in engaging with the audience/readers, to learn which aspects of their news raised curiosity and questions in readers' minds [11,12], and to understand whether readers are questioning the newsroom's journalistic integrity [13]. This knowledge is critical for learning what attracts readers to news content, targeting the right audience for news recommendations, building trust with the audience and so on [14,15]. According to Meier et al. [11], “a paradigm shift away from a ‘ lecturing ’ approach to a ‘ dialogue ’ approach is a key factor for journalism in a post-truth era”. Thus, there is a clear interest from both readers' and newsrooms' perspectives in engaging with each other in a dialogue fashion through question-answering [11,16].

With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) [17], the news media industry, like any other industry, is investigating how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and LLMs can be integrated with news production, distribution, audience engagement, and other related processes to improve efficiency, increase trust and accountability, and open new possibilities [18,19,20]. For instance, BBC has started experimenting with how bot technologies can be leveraged to reach new audiences on messaging platforms and social media [21,22]. They have developed a prototype of an in-article chatbot to help less engaged audiences understand big news stories [23]. Other media outlets have started experimenting with Meta (previously known as Facebook) chatbots [24]. While these experiments are ongoing individually in different newsrooms, facilitating question-answering (QA), one of the primary modes of interaction and dialogue in chatbots [25], remains a challenge for newsrooms [26,27]. While researchers are working towards mitigating technological limitations such as the lack of truthfulness and the existence of biased and formulaic text in LLM responses [28,29], we argue that it is also important to take a systematic approach to understanding how journalists and readers want to use a chatbot for question-answering and what roles they deem fit for such a chatbot. For instance, are journalists comfortable with a chatbot answering readers' questions about their news article? What types of questions do readers expect the chatbot to answer? And what types of questions do readers expect the authors to answer? Without answering these questions, we may end up designing QA chatbots that are detached from readers' and newsrooms' needs.

This paper takes a formative step towards designing LLM-powered chatbots that can answer open-ended questions from readers, reduce journalists' burden of answering a large number of queries, and at the same time elevate communication between readers and journalists. We call such chatbots QA chatbots. For the rest of the paper, we use the terms QA chatbots and chatbots interchangeably to refer to chatbots that are able to answer questions from news readers, unless specified otherwise. While we focus only on question-answering in the context of LLMs, in a real-world setting, like many LLM-powered chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT), a QA chatbot (or simply a chatbot) will likely have other forms of interaction (e.g., recommending news). To achieve our research agenda, we conducted two studies. First, we interviewed six professional journalists to understand how journalists currently answer questions from readers and, more broadly, interact with readers. The interviews revealed that most journalists now obtain feedback and answer questions from readers through one-to-one conversations over email, direct messages, or in-person meetups, except for a few member gatherings organized by news outlets. All participants were enthusiastic about using a QA chatbot as a mediator between themselves and readers. They want the chatbot to answer factual and redundant questions from readers, while directing questions that seek subjective interpretation towards them.

We subsequently conducted a between-subject experiment on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) with 124 participants with two goals: (1) understanding to what extent readers' perspectives and questioning patterns match how journalists see the functionalities of a QA chatbot; and (2) understanding how a QA chatbot might modulate readers' questioning patterns. The second goal is motivated by prior research showing that chatbots can significantly modulate user behaviour [30,31,32]. In the study, participants were instructed to read three articles from three different domains (health, politics, and environment) and ask questions to the authors of the articles or to a chatbot. We analyzed their responses using a grounded theory approach [33] and a set of quantitative measures. Our findings suggest that readers mostly asked questions in two broad categories: Information, questions that seek short-form factual and long-form details; and Interpretation, questions that seek explanation and opinion. We found that readers' questioning patterns differ significantly depending on the receiver - authors vs. chatbot. Participants asked questions seeking facts more frequently to the chatbot than to the authors, whereas they asked questions seeking explanation and opinion with multiple facets more frequently to the authors than to the chatbot.

These results indicate that readers' perspectives on the role of QA chatbots match journalists' views to some extent: readers, too, predominantly want the chatbot to answer factual questions while seeking to engage in subjective conversations with journalists. Despite this alignment, we found evidence that a significant number of readers do not share the view that chatbots should only answer factual questions. For instance, readers did ask a considerable number of questions seeking subjective interpretation to the chatbot, though not as frequently as to the authors. Similarly, a considerable number of readers wanted authors to answer factual as well as subjective questions. Finally, we found that chatbots can significantly modulate readers' behavior, which researchers and news organizations should be aware of. For example, articles with lower perceived quality motivated readers to be critical and question journalistic integrity when the authors were in the loop. However, when the chatbot was present, readers did not engage at the same level, even when the perceived quality of the news article was low.

Overall, these results indicate that researchers and news organizations need to thoroughly understand journalists' and readers' perspectives and expectations before determining the functionalities of a QA chatbot. The results also highlight the need to devise policies around chatbots and to communicate these policies effectively to journalists and readers. We conclude the paper by proposing a framework for devising a policy for designing QA chatbots for online news. In summary, our contributions are: (1) An interview study with six journalists to understand their current practices and challenges in answering questions from readers and how they perceive the role of an intelligent chatbot in this regard; (2) An online experiment with 124 participants to understand what questions readers typically ask about a news article and how these questions change if a chatbot, instead of the authors, is at the receiving end; and (3) A design framework for developing a chatbot policy, informed by the interviews, the online experiment, and a literature review.
